sentences.text: This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights, and daytime minutes count most: they raise a typical customer's chance of leaving steadily, from under 1% at 112 to about 13% at 249 minutes.

An international plan takes the chance from about 1% to about 13%, a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1%, and more voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1% at 0 to about 5% at 32 messages.
A higher international charge, more evening minutes, a higher evening charge and more night-time minutes also raise it steadily, each by one to two points.

Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1% in West Virginia to about 4% in California and in Washington, and to under 1% in Hawaii, Vermont and Colorado (41 to 80 training customers per state).
This part adds up two parts: customer-service calls combined with low daytime use, and a rise from 4 calls upwards.

Through it, daytime minutes lower the chance only while they stay below about 170 minutes (between 147 and 216 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: for a typical customer, from about 38% at 91 minutes to about 1% at 352 minutes.

With an evening charge above 17.12 US dollars, the chance is lowest at about 154 minutes of daytime use and higher either side: from about 1% at 112 minutes to about 17% at 249 minutes, against about 2% to about 10% at or below that charge.
Customer-service calls add to it from 4 calls upwards, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 3% at 0 calls to about 11% at 4 calls.

This part reads the voice-mail plan and a few states: through it, a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance by less than a point, and customers in states other than Alabama, North Carolina and West Virginia get about 2% instead of about 1%.

Through this part, evening minutes add nothing until about 239 minutes, then lower the chance steadily; it acts on 885 of 4000 training customers, 165 of whom left, and for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 5% without it and about 4% with it.

For a typical customer, the model gives a higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer is in California (about 6%) than if the customer is in West Virginia (about 1%) (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, total daytime minutes only clearly lowers the predicted chance that a customer leaves while it stays below about 170 minutes (between 147 and 216 minutes for different customers): for a typical such customer, going from 91 minutes to 352 minutes moves it from about 38% to about 1%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.

Through one part of the model, the customer-service calls only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves from 4 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 calls to 4 calls moves it from about 3% to about 11%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.
The model ignores total daytime charge, total evening calls, total international calls and total night-time charge.

record.summary: logit P(churn) = -1.05 + a sparse linear backbone over 40 inputs (day minutes +2.04 per SD, voicemail plan -0.90, international plan +0.76, international charge +0.71, voicemail messages +0.62, ...) + a service-call x low-day-usage gate + a 4+-calls hinge + an evening-minutes hinge + exactly linear voicemail and state-offset units, all additive in the logit. The gate is a low-day-minutes hinge whose kink moves up with each customer-service call (median 147 day minutes at 0 calls, 220 at 4, 276 at 6), so with the direct day-minutes edge the logit is V-shaped in day minutes and frequent callers with low usage churn. Service calls act only through hinges. Train AUC 0.901, accuracy 0.901.
